strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper builds a coherent narrative from phenomenon (attention dispersion) to mechanism (complexity-entropy correlation) to consequence (accuracy degradation) to method (contrastive attention masking).
CARVE is simple, training-free, and model-agnostic; it does not rely on external segmentation tools, making it practically attractive and easily reproducible.

Extensive empirical evidence: seven benchmarks (A-OKVQA, POPE, V*, TextVQA, DocVQA, ChartQA, ScienceQA), seven VLMs including very recent architectures (Qwen3-VL, Gemma-3), comparisons with concurrent training-free and trained baselines (ViCrop, SD-RPN) and external-tool approaches, plus latency/memory reporting.

Thorough ablations and validation: time-step selection, layer selection, threshold/region sensitivity (Fig. 7), component ablation (Table 4), multiplicative vs. additive contrast (Table 10), uniformity check via KL divergence (Table 11), decoding-temperature robustness (Table 8), and statistical significance tests (bootstrap CIs, McNemar's test) for the modest-size V* benchmark.

Honest and substantive limitations discussion, including a failure case on global spatial reasoning (BLINK depth) that precisely characterizes where the method breaks down, and acknowledgment of the idealized nature of the decomposition assumption (Sect. C preamble, Appendix J).
The analysis of complexity-entropy-accuracy relationships (Figs. 2-5) is a useful empirical contribution in its own right and directly motivates the method design.
weaknesses: The theoretical framework is largely idealized and post-hoc: Assumption 1 (multiplicative decomposition of attention into noise and semantic factors) is a strong simplification of softmax(QK^T) attention, and the 'closed-form solution' reduces to a regularized ratio. Theorems C.1-C.3 essentially restate the assumption rather than derive nontrivial properties, so the theoretical contribution is more design rationale than genuine theory.

The correlation analyses (Figs. 4-5) are observational; visual complexity, attention entropy, and task difficulty are confounded (complex images are intrinsically harder). The paper claims complexity 'impairs' reasoning via attention dispersion, but no interventional evidence (e.g., controlling for task difficulty) is provided to establish causation.

Novelty is incremental: contrasting attention maps between prompts and masking/cropping salient regions builds directly on ViCrop [38] and prior attention-based token pruning/grounding work; the main new elements are the general-instruction baseline map and the pixel-level contrast ratio, which are natural variations.

Some evidence is thin: the component ablation uses a 500-instance TextVQA subset, the sensitivity analysis uses 1,000 instances, and decoding-temperature robustness uses only 200 instances, limiting confidence in those specific conclusions.

Performance on DocVQA/ChartQA for LLaVA-1.5 models is extremely low (11-16 EM), suggesting the models are far below task capability; conclusions drawn on that regime may not generalize, and per-task hyperparameter sensitivity (layer range, p, K) is fixed rather than analyzed across tasks.

Overhead is significant: three forward passes (up to ~3x GPU time) and memory growth; while limitations acknowledge this and caching strategies are analyzed (Sect. C.4), the analysis is theoretical and the practical gains (~7-16% savings) are modest relative to the added cost.

The uniformity assumption for general-instruction attention is validated on average (KL 0.147) but, as the authors note, may weaken precisely on high-complexity images where the method is intended to help; this failure-mode interaction is not empirically characterized.

strengths: The empirical validation is unusually thorough for a training-free method: seven benchmarks, four main models plus three recent architectures (Qwen3-VL, Gemma-3) in the appendix, layer/time-step ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, component ablations, bootstrap confidence intervals, and McNemar's tests on the small V* benchmark. Consistent gains across this breadth are hard to dismiss as noise.

The phenomenon-to-mechanism-to-method narrative (visual complexity -> attention entropy -> accuracy degradation -> attention contrasting) is clearly structured and the motivating analysis in Sect. 3 (texture/color complexity metrics, entropy-accuracy and layer-wise entropy trends) is a genuine attempt to ground the design in observed behavior rather than to present CARVE as an unexplained heuristic.

The method is simple and reproducible: training-free, model-agnostic, with a closed-form contrast operation, released design choices (layer range, time-step weighting, threshold p, K), and detailed protocol descriptions including the OCR-free TextVQA setup.

The limitations section is substantive rather than perfunctory: it identifies the failure mode on global spatial reasoning (Fig. 11 BLINK example), the 3x inference overhead, and the idealized nature of the decomposition assumption, and includes a quantitative comparison of multiplicative vs. additive contrast.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is largely decorative. 'Assumption 1' is asserted, not derived; Theorem C.1 merely restates the assumption via a log transform, and Theorem C.2/C.3 are textbook algebra on a separable quadratic (strict convexity and closed-form minimum of a diagonal quadratic are trivial). The paper dresses a heuristic ratio A(Q)/(A(G)+λ) in the language of optimization theory; framing this as a 'theoretical foundation' overstates the contribution.

The central analysis in Sect. 3 establishes correlation, not causation, and this gap undermines the causal framing ('complex visual information impairs VLMs' reasoning performance via attention dispersion'). High entropy could be a symptom of hard samples rather than the cause of failure. The analysis is also conducted on a single model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B), no correlation coefficients or significance tests are reported for Figs. 4-5, and the complexity proxies (Canny edge density, hue entropy) confound clutter with image resolution, object size, and text density.

Novelty over the closest prior work (ViCrop and attention-based training-free cropping/masking lines) is incremental. Contrasting task-specific against generic-prompt attention is a natural variant of existing 'model knows where to look' analyses; the delta is pixel-level masking plus the λ-regularized ratio, and the paper's own ablation (direct masking +4.8% vs. full +9.3% on TextVQA) shows the base masking already captures much of the benefit. The comparison with baselines is limited to ViCrop and SD-RPN; other attention-based enhancement/token-pruning methods cited in related work are not compared.

Some experimental choices weaken the claims. LLaVA-1.5 gains on DocVQA/ChartQA start from near-failure baselines (11-14%), making large relative gains less meaningful. V* has only 191 samples. The complexity-entropy 'monotonic trend' in Fig. 4 is binned averages without dispersion, which can exaggerate linearity. Cherry-picked qualitative examples (Figs. 1, 8-10) complement but cannot substitute for failure-rate statistics on the masking step itself (e.g., how often CARVE masks the correct region).

The method is circular in a way the paper does not fully address: the same model's attention defines both the 'noise' and the 'signal', and the general instruction is selected by downstream accuracy (Table 9) rather than by the uniformity criterion the theory nominally requires. This makes the theoretical motivation partly post-hoc relative to the empirical design choices.

Compute overhead (~3x GPU time) is acknowledged but the practical value proposition is diluted by it, especially given that stronger recent models (Qwen3-VL) show diminishing benefits, suggesting the approach addresses a failure mode that newer architectures partially solve.

strengths: The paper builds a clear, well-motivated narrative: it empirically establishes the complexity→attention-entropy→accuracy chain (Sect. 3) before proposing the method, and the mechanism-level analysis (texture/color complexity vs. entropy, layer-wise entropy evolution) is more thorough than most training-free VLM enhancement papers.

CARVE is genuinely training-free and tool-free (no SAM/YOLO/CLIP dependency), which is a practical advantage over baselines; latency (Table 5) and GPU/memory overhead (Table 6) are transparently reported.

Evaluation is broad and convincing: four models in the main text, seven benchmarks, layer/time-step ablations, component ablations (Table 4), hyperparameter sensitivity (Fig. 7), multiplicative-vs-additive decomposition ablation (Table 10), and validation of the uniformity assumption via KL divergence (Table 11).
Statistical rigor is above average for this area: bootstrap CIs and McNemar's tests on the small V* benchmark (Tables 12–13), plus a decoding-temperature robustness check (Table 8).

Generalization is addressed with three additional recent models (Qwen3-VL, Gemma-3-27B) using an identical untuned pipeline (Table 14), which supports the claim that the mechanism persists across architectures.

Limitations are substantive and honest, including a concrete failure case on global spatial reasoning (Fig. 11) and an explicit statement of the 3-pass inference cost; the appendix properly flags the theory as motivational rather than exact.

The work is appropriate for its implicit contribution type (Algorithms/General with strong empirical analysis): it does not claim a new architecture, and the evidence standard—consistent gains across benchmarks and models—is met without requiring state-of-the-art on every dataset.
weaknesses: The theoretical component is thin. Theorem C.1 is essentially trivial: uniqueness of the decomposition follows directly from imposing the boundary condition Fsem(G,I)=1; the theorem does not establish that real attention satisfies this condition. Assumption 1 is admittedly a simplification of softmax(QK^T/√d), so the 'theoretical foundation' framing in Sect. 4.1 overstates what is proven; it is better viewed as a design rationale.

The central correlational analysis (Figs. 4–5) is confined to one model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B) on TextVQA, and edge-density/hue-entropy complexity metrics are crude proxies that also correlate with image type/content; the causal claim 'complex visual information impairs reasoning via attention dispersion' is only partially supported (the masking experiment uses hand-crafted masks and two anecdotal examples in Fig. 1).

Absolute gains on recent, capable models are modest (e.g., +8.9 on V* for Qwen2.5-VL-7B; +0.60 on ScienceQA; Table 14 shows a shrinking +2.21 for Gemma-3-27B), raising the question of how relevant the mechanism remains as VLM visual encoders improve.

The method requires ~3x vanilla inference time (1.0–1.3 s GPU time per sample) and the optimization analysis (Sect. C.4) yields only modest savings (~7–37% under idealized caching/early-termination), which limits deployment appeal; the proposed single-pass distillation is left as future work.

Layer/time-step configurations (L=[20,25], tend) appear to be tuned on the evaluated model families; the appendix shows a unified configuration works, but the sensitivity of the layer range to model depth/total layer count is not systematically analyzed for the newer architectures.

Overhead of three autoregressive passes plus attention storage means CARVE trades compute for accuracy; comparisons with training-based methods (SD-RPN) that amortize cost at inference time do not fully control for this asymmetry.
No explicit code release statement is included, which weakens reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter documentation.

Presentation has minor issues: red-text citations (e.g., Sect. 4.1, Eq. 9) appear unresolved in places, and Table 3's 'Relative Gain' mixed with absolute ▲ deltas can be confusing (relative percentages alongside absolute points).
